Tinker v. Des Moines. The 1969 Supreme Court decision holding that students do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate, protecting students' right to wear black armbands in school to protest the Vietnam War. In 1965, Des Moines high school students Mary Beth and John Tinker wore black armbands to school in protest of American military involvement in Vietnam. School officials suspended the students for violating a hastily adopted no-armband policy.

Justice Abe Fortas wrote that wearing armbands is symbolic speech protected by the First Amendment. Schools can restrict student speech only if it causes or threatens material and substantial disruption to school operations. That is a high bar to meet. The Court recognized that students retain constitutional rights and that schools cannot simply silence unpopular viewpoints. The decision became the foundation for student speech protection. Subsequent cases have carved out exceptions such as Hazelwood for school publications and Morse for drug-related speech. Tinker established that constitutional rights apply in schools, allowing symbolic speech as a category of First Amendment protection.
